TouchDesigner vs Blender: a live environment or a 3D suite?

By Syd Lawrence, a visual artist and developer who makes Vibresia. Facts last checked 2 November 2026; updated 2 November 2026.

If you want to build something that reacts live, to a show, a room or an installation, pick TouchDesigner: it is a node-based environment for real-time work, with MIDI, OSC, DMX, Syphon, Spout and NDI built in. If you want to model, animate and render, and want a suite that covers the whole 3D pipeline for nothing, pick Blender. Both run on macOS and Windows and both are free to start with, but they differ on one thing that matters here: TouchDesigner reads live audio and control signals, while Blender analyses a sound held in the file rather than what the computer is playing.

Control and connections

TouchDesignerBlender
MIDIYes: TouchDesigner reads MIDI with the MIDI In CHOP and sends MIDI with the MIDI Out CHOP, which can address any available MIDI device.No: Blender itself ships no MIDI input or output; MIDI input control is available through add-ons such as SimpleMIDI on the official Extensions platform.
OSCYes: TouchDesigner supports Open Sound Control through four operators, the OSC In CHOP and OSC Out CHOP for CHOP channels and the OSC In DAT and OSC Out DAT for raw messages, all over UDP.No: Blender has no built-in OSC, and OSC messaging is provided by community add-ons such as NodeOSC.
SyphonYes: Syphon is supported on macOS by the Syphon Spout In TOP and Syphon Spout Out TOP, which share textures with other applications through shared memory, with Syphon restricted to 8-bit RGBA.No: Blender has no native Syphon support; Syphon sharing is provided by the third-party TextureSharing add-on, whose own table notes the macOS client has performance issues.
SpoutYes: Spout is supported on Windows by the same two operators, and requires an Nvidia or AMD GPU because Intel does not work, with Spout limited by default to 10 active senders per computer.No: Blender has no native Spout support; Spout sharing is provided by the third-party TextureSharing add-on, whose own table notes the Windows receiver has performance issues.
NDIYes: NDI is built in as native operators, the NDI In TOP, NDI Out TOP and NDI DAT, using the NDI SDK bundled with each build, with no documented limit on frame rate or resolution beyond the hardware, while multi-cast configuration is done outside TouchDesigner with the separate NDI Access Manager tool.No: Blender has no native NDI support; NDI sending and receiving is provided by the third-party TextureSharing add-on across Windows, Linux and macOS.
DMXYes: The DMX Out CHOP sends channels to DMX, Art-Net, sACN, KiNET and FTDI devices, and a DMX In CHOP receives DMX, with DMX512 hardware limited to a 44Hz refresh rate.No: Blender has no built-in DMX support; the official Extensions platform hosts a DMX add-on for visualisation and programming with GDTF and MVR fixtures.
Video in and outYes: Video input comes from the Video Device In TOP for external cameras, capture cards, capture dongles, IP cameras and decoders, with several devices able to stream at once, while output goes to the screen, to SDI and HDMI cards via the Video Device Out TOP, or to TouchPlayer for standalone playback; the Non-Commercial licence caps image resolution at 1280x1280.Yes: Blender encodes rendered frames into video containers using FFmpeg and includes a video sequencer and compositor for editing, though it writes video to files rather than sending a live feed to other applications.

Every row comes from the app's own documentation, on the date shown in the sources below. "Not that we could find" means we could not find it documented, not that the app cannot do it.

Pick TouchDesigner if

you are building something live, on a Mac or a Windows machine, and you want MIDI, OSC, DMX, video in and video out without installing anyone else's add-on. The Non-Commercial licence is Free for learning, and Commercial is US$600 for paid work.

Pick Blender if

you are making 3D and animation and want one application that covers modelling, rigging, simulation, rendering and video editing, for nothing, with no licence to buy before a paid job.

Why people compare them

They are both free, both run on a Mac, and both end up on a laptop at a live show. But they are built around different ideas about what you make. Blender is the free and open source 3d creation suite, covering modelling, rigging, animation, simulation, rendering, compositing, motion tracking and video editing. TouchDesigner is derivative's node-based visual programming environment for real-time interactive media.

One makes finished images and films. The other makes systems that run while something else is happening. If you want a video, one of them is the answer. If you want visuals that answer the room, the other is.

Where TouchDesigner wins

The connections are built in. This is the difference that decides a live setup. TouchDesigner reads MIDI and sends it, sends and receives OSC, has Syphon on a Mac and Spout on Windows, has NDI, and has a DMX Out CHOP that sends to DMX, Art-Net, sACN, KiNET and FTDI devices. Blender has none of these itself: blender itself ships no MIDI input or output; MIDI input control is available through add-ons such as SimpleMIDI on the official Extensions platform., and the rest come from add-ons on the Extensions platform or from third parties.

It hears what is playing. TouchDesigner takes audio input live and can drive parameters from it, and it takes MIDI and OSC to change them while it runs. Blender cannot do the equivalent: blender cannot drive visuals from live system audio, because its frequency analysis node samples a sound data-block held in the file at a given point in time rather than an incoming signal.

It has a player for the output. TouchPlayer runs a TouchDesigner file on another machine, and video input comes from the Video Device In TOP for external cameras, capture cards, capture dongles, IP cameras and decoders, with several devices able to stream at once, while output goes to the screen, to SDI and HDMI cards via the Video Device Out TOP, or to TouchPlayer for standalone playback; the Non-Commercial licence caps image resolution at 1280x1280.

Where Blender wins

It is free for paid work. It runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and the official requirements page describes it as cross-platform with a portable install that needs no internet connection. Its licence page states that Blender can be used commercially by artists and studios and that what you create is yours alone, with no registration and no internet connection. TouchDesigner's free licence is Free and it rules out paid work and caps output at 1280x1280.

It covers the whole pipeline. It covers the entire 3D pipeline in one application, from modelling and rigging through animation, simulation, rendering, compositing and motion tracking, and it includes video editing and game asset creation

It is three platforms. Blender runs on Mac, Windows, Linux, so the same project opens on whatever the studio has. TouchDesigner runs on Windows, Mac.

It has three engines. It ships a realtime render engine in EEVEE, a fast preview engine in Workbench and a path tracer in Cycles, so the same scene can be previewed live and rendered at high quality

Where both fall short

Neither is small. Blender's download is listed at 330 MB for the macOS disk image and 349 MB for the Windows installer, and The stated minimum machine is 8GB of RAM with a GPU offering 2GB of VRAM and OpenGL 4.3 or Vulkan 1.3, with 32GB of RAM recommended, and a 1920 by 1080 display is advised for live use. TouchDesigner is a full environment too, and it wants a machine that can run it.

Both are built to be driven by a person. Neither plays by itself. Blender wants a scene built and then rendered; TouchDesigner wants a network of nodes built and then run. Either way, the result is only as good as the work you put in.

Neither is a music visualiser. Both are general tools, and both expect you to bring the content and decide how it reacts. If what you want is visuals that react to what the Mac is playing, with nothing to prepare, that is a different job than either of these does.

What it costs

Blender is free. That is the whole price: Free, and its licence lets studios use it commercially. The paid parts of the Blender world are training, production assets and support, sold by Blender Studio as a subscription, not the software itself.

TouchDesigner's Non-Commercial licence is Free for personal use and learning, capped at 1280x1280 output. Commercial is US$600, one-time for paid projects, Educational is US$300, one-time and Pro is US$2,200, one-time, which adds six hours of Pro Support. Derivative lists those as from prices.

Questions people ask

Is Blender better than TouchDesigner for live visuals?

For a live system that reacts to sound and control signals, TouchDesigner is the better tool: its MIDI, OSC, DMX and video connections are built in and it reads live audio. For modelling, animation and finished renders, Blender is the better tool by a distance, and it is free for commercial work.

Can Blender react to music?

Not live. blender itself ships no MIDI input or output; MIDI input control is available through add-ons such as SimpleMIDI on the official Extensions platform. Blender analyses the sound in the file, so making it react to a live input means routing that input into it yourself.

Can I use Blender for commercial work?

Yes. Blender is free and open source under the GNU General Public License, and its licence page states that it can be used commercially by artists and studios. TouchDesigner's free Non-Commercial licence is the one that rules out paid work.

Do they run on the same computers?

Both run on a Mac and on Windows, and Blender also runs on Linux. Blender needs Apple silicon with macOS 13 Ventura or later and 8GB of RAM, or Windows 8.1 or later; Blender 4.5 LTS is the last release to support Intel Macs, and TouchDesigner needs macOS 13 or later on a 2020-or-later Mac (Apple silicon highly recommended).
